content: The document outlines detailed procedures and guidelines for the verification of the elimination of human onchocerciasis (river blindness) in endemic countries. Below is a professional summary of the key points: 1. Declaration of Interests by Participants: Participants involved in the verification process declared their personal and institutional interests. Most participants reported no conflicts of interest, except for a few who disclosed past research grants or consulting roles. For example, Mark Eberhard disclosed a research grant from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation that ended in May 2014, and Thomas Unnasch disclosed consulting fees and committee memberships related to onchocerciasis elimination efforts. 2. Country Dossier Requirements: Countries seeking verification of onchocerciasis elimination must submit a comprehensive dossier to the World Health Organization (WHO). This dossier should include historical, epidemiological, and programmatic information, such as: The history of onchocerciasis in the country, including how the disease was introduced and its geographic distribution. Demographic and ethnographic data on affected populations. Economic activities in endemic regions and migration patterns. Information on the primary and secondary vectors of Onchocerca volvulus and their distribution. Details of the healthcare infrastructure in endemic areas. 3. Treatment Coverage and Surveillance: The dossier must demonstrate that at least 75% of the total population (or 80–85% of the eligible population) in endemic communities received ivermectin treatment during each treatment round. It should also include data from in-depth epidemiological and entomological surveys, as well as pre-treatment and post-treatment evaluations. 4. National Elimination Program Overview: A detailed description of the national elimination program is required, including: Participating organizations and their roles. National policies and interventions implemented against onchocerciasis. 5. Verification Process: The verification process begins with the submission of a letter and dossier to the WHO Director-General. If the dossier is deemed adequate, an International Verification Team (IVT) is appointed. The IVT reviews the dossier, conducts country visits if necessary, and evaluates the reliability of the elimination claim. The IVT report includes conclusions on whether elimination has been achieved, along with recommendations for post-elimination surveillance or additional steps if elimination criteria are not met. 6. Entomological Monitoring: Monitoring the infection rates of black flies (Simulium species) with Onchocerca volvulus larvae is a key method for evaluating the impact of ivermectin distribution. This approach is preferred over parasitological evaluations in humans due to its sensitivity and non-invasive nature. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technology is recommended for detecting parasite DNA in black flies, as it is more efficient and cost-effective than traditional dissection methods. Fly collections are grouped into pools and tested for the presence of O. volvulus larvae. The results are analyzed using statistical software to determine infection rates and transmission potential. 7. Post-Elimination Surveillance: Countries must establish robust post-elimination surveillance systems to monitor for potential reintroduction of the parasite. This includes mechanisms for detecting and responding to new cases and maintaining community awareness. 8. International Verification Team (IVT): The IVT consists of experts in onchocerciasis control and elimination, including entomologists. Members must be independent, with no recent involvement in the applicant country’s program. Observers may provide technical input but cannot directly influence national authorities without WHO consultation. 9. Country Visits: If required, the IVT conducts visits to endemic areas to assess program operations, interview personnel and community members, and verify the accuracy of the data. The visit typically lasts at least five working days, depending on the number of endemic foci. 10. IVT Report: The IVT report includes an executive summary, methodology, critical discussions, conclusions, and recommendations. It evaluates compliance with WHO elimination criteria and provides guidance for future steps if elimination has not been achieved. 11. Entomological Data Collection and Analysis: Entomological evaluations involve collecting black flies, identifying species, and testing for parasite DNA. The methodology has been standardized across programs in Africa and the Americas. Data on biting rates, infection rates, and annual transmission potential are essential for assessing the interruption of parasite transmission. 12. Advantages of Entomological Monitoring: Monitoring black fly infection rates provides rapid and sensitive indicators of community microfilarial load reduction. The process is non-invasive and well-accepted by communities, with the added benefit of delivering health messages to increase ivermectin coverage. 13. Post-Treatment Surveillance: Surveillance systems must monitor for renewed transmission, particularly in areas with competent vectors and high biting densities. Fly collections and PCR testing are used to detect any evidence of parasite-vector contact. This document provides a comprehensive framework for verifying the elimination of onchocerciasis, emphasizing rigorous data collection, independent evaluation, and sustained post-elimination monitoring.
